title: Help without being seen
hookLine: Maimonides' ladder of giving ranks anonymous giving near the top (Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10)

cards: Be honest: when you do something kind, is a small part of you hoping someone notices? The post about the fundraiser. The casual mention that you helped a friend move.

That's human. But it raises a real question: does it matter who sees? In twelfth-century Egypt, a rabbi and doctor named Moses Maimonides wrote a great code of Jewish law, and in it he took giving apart like a watchmaker.
He ranked it, rung by rung, from grudging to best. And near the very top sits a gift nobody sees.

teach.b: In Hebrew, the word for this kind of giving is tzedakah, from the root for justice, not just kindness: giving is part of setting things right.
In his code, the Mishneh Torah, in the laws of gifts to the poor, Maimonides lays out eight levels. At the bottom: giving grudgingly. A little higher: giving gladly, but less than you should.
Higher: giving before you're asked. Then the rungs about who knows.
Next, the poor person knows who gave, but the giver doesn't know who received: he tells of sages who tied coins in a cloth behind their backs so the poor could take them unseen.
Higher: the giver knows, but the receiver doesn't, like sages who slipped coins through a doorway and left.
Near the top, neither knows the other. He recalls a chamber in the ancient Temple where people left gifts in secret and the poor were supported in secret. Why does hiddenness matter so much?

teach.h: DIGNITY FOR THE ONE WHO RECEIVES.
teach.b: It protects the dignity of the person receiving: no one has to look up at you, or feel they owe you. And it keeps the giver from turning kindness into a performance.
One rung sits higher still: helping someone stand on their own, with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they never need the gift at all.
Jesus says something close in the Gospels: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Two teachers, each in their own world, both pointing at the quiet gift.

how: Jews give tzedakah in many forms, and Maimonides counts giving into a trustworthy community fund as close to the secret gift; people of every faith also give anonymously for the same reasons.

games.q: you're a sage in Maimonides' story. you want to give to a poor family without shaming them. what do you do?
o: hand the money over in the market square.
slip coins through their doorway and leave.
announce your gift at the synagogue.
games.why: some sages slipped coins through doorways and walked away, so the family never had to face them. higher still: neither knows the other.

practice: Think of a need you could meet without your name on it: paying for the coffee of the person behind you, an unsigned donation, groceries left on a porch. Picture doing it, and walking away.
Notice the small itch to tell someone, let it be there, and let it go unanswered.

wordCard.voice: Tzedakah, the Hebrew word for this kind of giving, rooted in justice rather than mere kindness. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, tzedakah: charity, from tzedek, justice. giving as righteousness, not just generosity.

carryVoice: Your line: unseen. A hidden gift guards the dignity of the one who receives it. See you tomorrow.
